screens.title: Conditional Logic and Loops for Game Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how scripts make decisions and repeat actions inside a game. Conditional logic lets your code choose different paths — for example, triggering Game Over when health reaches zero or giving a power-up when a player collects a special item. Loops let you perform repeated tasks such as spawning many enemies, iterating through game objects, or running timed behaviors. We'll study the core tools: if, else if, else, switch, comparison and logical operators, and for and while loops. You will see clear C# examples drawn from player health, damage types, and a simple score-based level system. Along the way we'll point out common mistakes, like using assignment instead of comparison, and the hazard of infinite loops in runtime code. By the end you should be able to pick the right control structure for health checks, scoring thresholds, enemy patterns, and iteration across collections. Think about a damaging hit in your game: which conditional or loop will express that behavior reliably and safely?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Conditional Logic & Loops
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Conditional Logic & Loops

Learn to make decisions with conditionals and handle repetition with loops to implement core gameplay behaviors like damage, spawning, and scoring.

16:9 HD Classroom
Decision Making

Use if, else if, else and switch to choose behaviors such as Game Over or power-up effects.

Repetition & Loops

Use for and while to spawn objects, iterate enemies, or run countdowns safely to avoid infinite loops.

Explore Key Topics
Conditionals

Make decisions with if, else if, else and logical operators.

Switch

Handle distinct choices like damage types concisely using switch and case.

Loops

Repeat tasks with for and while; be mindful of loop termination to avoid freezes.

Visual Concept
Cards represent decision points and repeated actions that form common gameplay flows.
Trigger

Player collides with enemy → evaluate damage conditions.

Loop

For each enemy in scene → alert or change state.

Orientation

This chapter focuses on writing clear conditions and safe loops that respond to player state and iterate over game data. Expect code examples in C# for Unity and practical troubleshooting advice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over this chapter you will build four practical skills that map directly to game mechanics. First, you will implement conditional statements to control game flow: writing if, else if, and else blocks so your game reacts to player health, timers, and item pickups. Second, you will use comparison and logical operators to form expressive boolean conditions — combining checks with AND, OR, and NOT to represent nuanced states. Third, you will learn to apply switch statements when a single variable needs several distinct handlers, such as different damage types or level actions. Fourth, you will construct for and while loops to repeat tasks like spawning, iterating enemies, or implementing timed effects while being mindful of loop termination to prevent infinite freezes. Each objective includes a short explanation, why it matters, and a micro-mnemonic to help you remember when to use each tool.

screens.title: If Statements — Basic Decision Making
screens.narratorSegment: An if statement is the simplest decision tool in your scripts. It evaluates a boolean expression — something that resolves to true or false — and executes a block of code only when that expression is true. For example, checking if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero and then triggering a Game Over screen is an if-style decision. Use if for single checks or to short-circuit behavior early, such as returning from a method if the player is already dead. A common pattern is to guard a method with a quick if that returns early, making the rest of the method assume a valid state. Concrete example: when applying damage you might first check if currentHealth is already zero to avoid double processing. A common misconception is thinking an if will automatically handle multiple ranges; when you need ordered checks, combine if with else if and else. Another mistake is placing heavy work inside the condition itself; keep the condition a clear expression about state, and leave side effects inside the block. Takeaway: use if for explicit, single-condition gates, and favor clear, readable boolean expressions so your game state remains predictable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › If Statements
Definition

An if evaluates a boolean expression. If it is true, the block executes. Use it to gate behavior like death checks and early returns.

Example
// Example guard
if (currentHealth <= 0)
{
  Debug.Log("Player is already defeated.");
  return;
}
Common Mistake

Using assignment inside the condition by mistake. In C#, use double equals for comparison, not a single equals which assigns a value and will not compile in this context.

Key Takeaway

Keep conditions readable and side effects inside the block; use if for single-state checks and early returns.

Teaching Visual
Scenario: Apply Damage

When TakeDamage is called, first check if the player is already defeated to avoid applying further damage or playing extra effects.

Check Your Understanding

Why is an early return helpful? It prevents redundant work and keeps method logic simple and safe.

screens.title: Else If Chains — Ordered Conditions
screens.narratorSegment: Else if allows you to test multiple ordered conditions so only the first true branch runs. This matters for ranges and tiered responses: for example, awarding tiers for a score or selecting enemy behavior based on remaining health. Conditions are evaluated top to bottom, so the order matters. A good pattern is to check the most specific or highest priority condition first. The chapter gives a scoring example: check if score is greater than or equal to 1000 for Gold, else if score is greater than or equal to 500 for Silver, else Bronze. If you reverse that order, the highest tier may never be reached because an earlier condition swallowed it. A concrete game example is enemy behavior by health percentage: check aggressive behavior when health is above 50 first, then defensive between 25 and 50, and finally flee below 25. A common misconception is thinking that multiple else if blocks can all run; by design only one branch executes. Takeaway: design the chain order to reflect priority and exclusivity so your game produces predictable single outcomes. Else If Chains — Ordered Conditions means use ordered else if checks for exclusive ranges and prioritized responses; the first true branch runs and others are skipped.. In practical terms, check ranges and pick the first matching action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Else If Chains
Pattern
if (score >= 1000)
{
  Debug.Log("Gold Tier!");
}
else if (score >= 500)
{
  Debug.Log("Silver Tier!");
}
else
{
  Debug.Log("Bronze Tier.");
}
This structure ensures only one tier prints per score check. Order conditions from highest to lowest priority to avoid incorrect matches.
Scenario: Enemy Health Ranges
If an enemy's health is above 50 percent, attack aggressively. Else if between 25 and 50 inclusive, switch to a defensive stance. Else, flee. The order prevents overlapping ranges from causing conflicting behaviors.
Check

If you placed the 'flee' condition first, low-health behavior could be evaluated incorrectly for higher ranges. Always reason about overlaps before writing the chain.

screens.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators compare values and return a boolean. Use equal, not equal, greater than, less than, and their inclusive variants to express conditions about numbers, enums, and other comparable values. Logical operators combine these comparisons into compound checks. Use AND when all conditions must be true, OR when any condition suffices, and NOT to invert a boolean. For instance, checking if the player is alive and an enemy is close can be written with an AND: playerIsAlive && enemyIsClose. A concrete example from the chapter: if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero OR outOfTime, then the game is over. One misconception is overcomplicating expressions without grouping; use parentheses to make intent clear, especially when mixing AND and OR because operator precedence can lead to unexpected results. Also be careful comparing floating point values for equality in physics contexts; prefer ranges. Takeaway: pick comparisons that reflect game state precisely and combine them with logical operators and parentheses to express intent cleanly. Comparison and Logical Operators means use comparison operators to form basic checks and logical operators to combine them. parentheses clarify intent.. In practical terms, combine checks with ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and &&, ||, !. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Comparison & Logical Ops
Reference
  • == equal to — check values match
  • != not equal to
  • < > <= >= comparisons for ordering
  • && AND — both must be true
  • || OR — at least one is true
  • ! NOT — invert a boolean
Example
if (playerIsAlive && (enemyIsClose || playerHasShield))
{
  // engage combat or block
}
Misconception

Assuming && and || have the same precedence. Use parentheses to make the intended grouping explicit, for example when combining health and timer checks with either-or conditions.

Pro Tip

When debugging complex boolean logic, log intermediate sub-expressions so you can see which part of the condition is failing or passing.

screens.title: Switch Statements — Multi-Case Handling
screens.narratorSegment: A switch statement tests a single expression against multiple case values and routes execution to the matching case. In game code this shines when you have discrete types or enumerations, such as damage kinds: Physical, Fire, Ice, Poison. Each case can apply different effects: fire may double damage, ice may halve it, poison could apply over time. The chapter's PlayerHealth example uses a switch on DamageType to adjust currentHealth depending on the type. Important practical notes: end each case with a break to avoid fall-through unless fall-through is intentional. Include a default case to handle unexpected values and log a warning. A misconception is using switch when ranges are needed; switch equals exact matches and is not ideal for numeric ranges without advanced pattern matching. Takeaway: use switch for tidy, readable handling of distinct, enumerable choices like power-up types or level states and keep cases small and focused for maintainability. Switch Statements — Multi-Case Handling means use switch to cleanly dispatch different behaviors for discrete values; include default and break statements for clarity.. In practical terms, replace long else-if chains when a single variable has distinct values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Switch Statement

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Switch
PlayerHealth: DamageType Switch
switch (type)
{
  case DamageType.Physical:
    currentHealth -= amount;
    break;
  case DamageType.Fire:
    currentHealth -= amount * 2;
    break;
  case DamageType.Ice:
    currentHealth -= amount / 2;
    break;
  case DamageType.Poison:
    currentHealth -= amount / 4;
    break;
  default:
    Debug.LogWarning("Unknown damage type received.");
    break;
}
Why Use Switch?

Switch makes code easier to scan when the same variable has several discrete handlers. It reduces the mental overhead compared to long else-if chains and groups related behavior together.

Misconception

Switch is not ideal for numeric ranges unless your language supports pattern matching; prefer ordered else-if for ranges.

screens.title: For Loops — Fixed Iteration
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop runs a block a fixed number of times when you know the number of iterations ahead of time. It has three parts: initialization, condition, and iteration. Use it to spawn a fixed count of enemies, step through an array by index, or check thresholds such as levelUp checks. The chapter example uses a for loop both to simulate healing over a number of seconds (not recommended in real Update code) and to check level-up thresholds in PlayerScore. Concrete example: for i from zero to threshold length, if score reaches the threshold for the next level and the player is at that level, increment the level and break the loop. A common pitfall is off-by-one errors: ensure your condition uses the correct inequality to cover the intended indices. Also avoid heavy blocking work inside for loops on the main thread; use coroutines or timed updates for real-time repeated effects. Takeaway: use for when the iteration count is known and manage loop body performance to keep frame rates smooth. For Loops — Fixed Iteration means choose for loops when you know the exact iteration count and index-based access is needed, like spawning or threshold checks.. In practical terms, repeat a block a known number of times, ideal for spawning or indexing arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › For Loops
Structure
for (int i = 0; i < levelUpThresholds.Length; i++)
{
  if (score >= levelUpThresholds[i] && level == (i + 1))
  {
    level++;
    Debug.Log("Congratulations! You reached Level " + level + "!");
    break;
  }
}
Note the break after leveling up: it avoids unnecessary checks and ensures only one promotion per check cycle.
Example: Spawn Enemies
Use a for loop to spawn an exact number of enemies, indexing the spawn positions. If you need timing between spawns, use a coroutine instead of a blocking for loop in Update to avoid freezing the game.
Misconception

A for loop that runs heavy work on the main thread can lower frame rate. Move longer operations out of Update or into coroutines.

screens.title: While & Do-While — Condition-Based Repetition
screens.narratorSegment: While loops repeat a block as long as a condition remains true. They are appropriate when you don't know the exact iteration count ahead of time, but you must ensure the condition will eventually become false. The do-while variant guarantees the body runs at least once before the condition is checked. In games, using a raw while loop on the main thread for time-based or frame-dependent behavior can freeze the editor if the condition never becomes false; instead, favor coroutines or update-driven logic. The chapter warns about infinite loops: if the condition never changes, your game will hang. A concrete example is a conceptual healing loop that iterates over durationInSeconds to simulate healing per second — the example in the PlayerHealth script shows such a loop is illustrative but not appropriate for real-time Update code. Takeaway: choose while when you need condition-driven repetition, but design an exit or use frame-friendly constructs to avoid blocking the game. While & Do-While — Condition-Based Repetition means use while for condition-based repetition and do-while to run at least once. avoid blocking the main thread; prefer coroutines for timed behavior.. In practical terms, repeat as long as a condition holds; watch for infinite loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › While & Do-While
Pattern
while (playerHealth > 0)
{
  // game continues
  // ensure something makes playerHealth reach zero at some point
}

// do-while example
int i = 0;
do
{
  i++;
} while (i < 3);
Ensure the loop body changes the condition or add a counter with a safe upper bound. For time-based repetition prefer coroutines to avoid blocking frames.
Infinite Loop Caution

An infinite loop will freeze your game and editor. Always reason about the loop's termination and test in a safe environment. When in doubt, add a fallback counter or timeout check.

screens.title: PlayerHealth Walkthrough — Applying Conditionals & Switch
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the PlayerHealth example to see conditionals and switch used together. The script initializes currentHealth to maxHealth and hides the Game Over panel. TakeDamage begins with an if that returns early if currentHealth is already zero — this prevents applying damage twice to the defeated player. The switch on DamageType then alters how much health is subtracted depending on type: physical applies the base amount, fire doubles it, ice halves it, and poison applies a smaller immediate hit. After modification, code clamps currentHealth to a minimum of zero to avoid negative health values. Finally, another if-else if checks for game over when currentHealth is zero, or a critical warning state when currentHealth falls below one quarter of maxHealth. Concrete example: taking 20 fire damage subtracts 40 from currentHealth in the provided model. A common misconception is expecting switch to perform range checks — it only matches explicit values. Takeaway: use early guards, switch for type-based adjustments, and clamp health values to keep state sane. In practical terms, a careful walk through takedamage, switch, and game over checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PlayerHealth Walkthrough
Key Excerpts
public void TakeDamage(int amount, DamageType type)
{
  if (currentHealth <= 0)
  {
    Debug.Log("Player is already defeated.");
    return;
  }

  switch (type)
  {
    case DamageType.Physical:
      currentHealth -= amount;
      break;
    // other cases...
  }

  currentHealth = Mathf.Max(0, currentHealth);

  if (currentHealth <= 0)
  {
    TriggerGameOver();
  }
  else if (currentHealth < maxHealth / 4)
  {
    Debug.LogWarning("Player health is critically low!");
  }
}
Explanation
  • Early return prevents double-damage and simplifies logic.
  • Switch cleanly handles damage type differences.
  • Clamping with Max prevents negative health values.
  • Ordered if/else if chooses game over before warning states.
Key Takeaway

Combine guards, switch, clamping, and ordered checks to make health systems robust and predictable.

PlayerScore Excerpt
public void AddScore(int amount)
{
  score += amount;
  Debug.Log("Score: " + score);
  CheckLevelUp();
}

void CheckLevelUp()
{
  for (int i = 0; i < levelUpThresholds.Length; i++)
  {
    if (score >= levelUpThresholds[i] && level == (i + 1))
    {
      level++;
      Debug.Log("Congratulations! You reached Level " + level + "!");
      break;
    }
  }
}

  • Use arrays for thresholds so designers can tweak level costs without code changes.
  • Break after leveling up to prevent over-incrementing in a single evaluation.
  • Use switch to trigger level-specific effects like unlocking skills or visual feedback.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how scripts make decisions and repeat actions inside a game. Conditional logic lets your code choose different paths — for example, triggering Game Over when health reaches zero or giving a power-up when a player collects a special item. Loops let you perform repeated tasks such as spawning many enemies, iterating through game objects, or running timed behaviors. We'll study the core tools: if, else if, else, switch, comparison and logical operators, and for and while loops. You will see clear C# examples drawn from player health, damage types, and a simple score-based level system. Along the way we'll point out common mistakes, like using assignment instead of comparison, and the hazard of infinite loops in runtime code. By the end you should be able to pick the right control structure for health checks, scoring thresholds, enemy patterns, and iteration across collections. Think about a damaging hit in your game: which conditional or loop will express that behavior reliably and safely?

Over this chapter you will build four practical skills that map directly to game mechanics. First, you will implement conditional statements to control game flow: writing if, else if, and else blocks so your game reacts to player health, timers, and item pickups. Second, you will use comparison and logical operators to form expressive boolean conditions — combining checks with AND, OR, and NOT to represent nuanced states. Third, you will learn to apply switch statements when a single variable needs several distinct handlers, such as different damage types or level actions. Fourth, you will construct for and while loops to repeat tasks like spawning, iterating enemies, or implementing timed effects while being mindful of loop termination to prevent infinite freezes. Each objective includes a short explanation, why it matters, and a micro-mnemonic to help you remember when to use each tool.

In the practical portion you'll implement two small systems: a PlayerHealth script that handles damage and game over logic, and a PlayerScore system that triggers level-up actions when thresholds are reached. You'll use if-else chains to check health boundaries, switch statements to vary damage by type, and a for loop to check or spawn multiple objects. The hands-on activity walks through attaching scripts to GameObjects, setting tags and colliders, and testing triggers in the Unity editor. This makes the theory concrete: you will actually see score increase messages and level-up debug output in the Console, and you will observe the Game Over panel appear when health hits zero. Completing these tasks verifies you can apply conditionals and loops to real gameplay scenarios and recognize basic runtime pitfalls like infinite loops or improper comparisons.

An if statement is the simplest decision tool in your scripts. It evaluates a boolean expression — something that resolves to true or false — and executes a block of code only when that expression is true. For example, checking if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero and then triggering a Game Over screen is an if-style decision. Use if for single checks or to short-circuit behavior early, such as returning from a method if the player is already dead. A common pattern is to guard a method with a quick if that returns early, making the rest of the method assume a valid state. Concrete example: when applying damage you might first check if currentHealth is already zero to avoid double processing. A common misconception is thinking an if will automatically handle multiple ranges; when you need ordered checks, combine if with else if and else. Another mistake is placing heavy work inside the condition itself; keep the condition a clear expression about state, and leave side effects inside the block. Takeaway: use if for explicit, single-condition gates, and favor clear, readable boolean expressions so your game state remains predictable.

Else if allows you to test multiple ordered conditions so only the first true branch runs. This matters for ranges and tiered responses: for example, awarding tiers for a score or selecting enemy behavior based on remaining health. Conditions are evaluated top to bottom, so the order matters. A good pattern is to check the most specific or highest priority condition first. The chapter gives a scoring example: check if score is greater than or equal to 1000 for Gold, else if score is greater than or equal to 500 for Silver, else Bronze. If you reverse that order, the highest tier may never be reached because an earlier condition swallowed it. A concrete game example is enemy behavior by health percentage: check aggressive behavior when health is above 50 first, then defensive between 25 and 50, and finally flee below 25. A common misconception is thinking that multiple else if blocks can all run; by design only one branch executes. Takeaway: design the chain order to reflect priority and exclusivity so your game produces predictable single outcomes. Else If Chains — Ordered Conditions means use ordered else if checks for exclusive ranges and prioritized responses; the first true branch runs and others are skipped.. In practical terms, check ranges and pick the first matching action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison operators compare values and return a boolean. Use equal, not equal, greater than, less than, and their inclusive variants to express conditions about numbers, enums, and other comparable values. Logical operators combine these comparisons into compound checks. Use AND when all conditions must be true, OR when any condition suffices, and NOT to invert a boolean. For instance, checking if the player is alive and an enemy is close can be written with an AND: playerIsAlive && enemyIsClose. A concrete example from the chapter: if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero OR outOfTime, then the game is over. One misconception is overcomplicating expressions without grouping; use parentheses to make intent clear, especially when mixing AND and OR because operator precedence can lead to unexpected results. Also be careful comparing floating point values for equality in physics contexts; prefer ranges. Takeaway: pick comparisons that reflect game state precisely and combine them with logical operators and parentheses to express intent cleanly. Comparison and Logical Operators means use comparison operators to form basic checks and logical operators to combine them. parentheses clarify intent.. In practical terms, combine checks with ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and &&, ||, !. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A switch statement tests a single expression against multiple case values and routes execution to the matching case. In game code this shines when you have discrete types or enumerations, such as damage kinds: Physical, Fire, Ice, Poison. Each case can apply different effects: fire may double damage, ice may halve it, poison could apply over time. The chapter's PlayerHealth example uses a switch on DamageType to adjust currentHealth depending on the type. Important practical notes: end each case with a break to avoid fall-through unless fall-through is intentional. Include a default case to handle unexpected values and log a warning. A misconception is using switch when ranges are needed; switch equals exact matches and is not ideal for numeric ranges without advanced pattern matching. Takeaway: use switch for tidy, readable handling of distinct, enumerable choices like power-up types or level states and keep cases small and focused for maintainability. Switch Statements — Multi-Case Handling means use switch to cleanly dispatch different behaviors for discrete values; include default and break statements for clarity.. In practical terms, replace long else-if chains when a single variable has distinct values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A for loop runs a block a fixed number of times when you know the number of iterations ahead of time. It has three parts: initialization, condition, and iteration. Use it to spawn a fixed count of enemies, step through an array by index, or check thresholds such as levelUp checks. The chapter example uses a for loop both to simulate healing over a number of seconds (not recommended in real Update code) and to check level-up thresholds in PlayerScore. Concrete example: for i from zero to threshold length, if score reaches the threshold for the next level and the player is at that level, increment the level and break the loop. A common pitfall is off-by-one errors: ensure your condition uses the correct inequality to cover the intended indices. Also avoid heavy blocking work inside for loops on the main thread; use coroutines or timed updates for real-time repeated effects. Takeaway: use for when the iteration count is known and manage loop body performance to keep frame rates smooth. For Loops — Fixed Iteration means choose for loops when you know the exact iteration count and index-based access is needed, like spawning or threshold checks.. In practical terms, repeat a block a known number of times, ideal for spawning or indexing arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

While loops repeat a block as long as a condition remains true. They are appropriate when you don't know the exact iteration count ahead of time, but you must ensure the condition will eventually become false. While loops repeat based on a condition but must include a termination path to avoid infinite loops.
